# 5.1 Conditional Filter Operators

> "A query filter narrows results to documents matching specific field values or query operators (e.g. $gt, $lt, $in). An empty filter ({}) matches every document."

## 1. Core Concept & Everyday Mental Model

Sometimes you want to search for more than an exact match. You use MongoDB query operators inside `find()` for this job. Every query operator starts with a dollar sign `$`. They let you compare numbers, check lists, or combine rules.

Look at the diagram above to see the three operator groups. Comparison operators check greater-than or less-than rules. Array operators (`$in`, `$nin`) check lists of values. Logical operators (`$or`, `$and`) join multiple conditions together.

Conditional operators are like smart search filters on a store website. You need not search for one exact price. Instead, you can search for prices above a number (`$gt`). You can also match a list (`$in`) or combine rules (`$or`).

## 2. Step-by-Step Command Breakdown

### 2.1 Relational Comparison: `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$ne`

Place comparison operators inside curly braces after the field name. For example, write `{ age: { $gte: 18 } }`. Here, `$gt` means greater than and `$gte` means greater or equal. Also, `$lt` means less than, `$lte` means less or equal, and `$ne` means not equal.

### 2.2 Set Membership (`$in`, `$nin`) & Logical (`$or`, `$and`)

Use `$in` with a list in square brackets, like `{ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } }`. It matches any value inside that list. Conversely, `$nin` matches values not in the list. Use `$or` when at least one rule must be true. Use `$and` when all rules must be true.

## 3. Hands-On MongoDB Shell (`mongosh`) Examples

Practice typing these commands in `mongosh`. Read each comment to see how the command works.

```javascript
// 1. Greater than or equal to ($gte)
db.students.find({ age: { $gte: 18 } });

// 2. Match any value in a list ($in)
db.students.find({ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } });

// 3. Match if EITHER condition is true ($or)
db.students.find({
  $or: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }]
});
```

Each command follows the exact textbook rules. Notice how clean the JSON objects look.

Keep this simple flow in mind during exams. Next, review the table and key rules below.

## 5. Summary Table & Beginner Rules to Remember

| Operator | Meaning | Simple Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `$gt` / `$gte` | Greater than (`>`) / Greater than or equal (`>=`) | `{ age: { $gte: 18 } }` |
| `$lt` / `$lte` | Less than (`<`) / Less than or equal (`<=`) | `{ age: { $lt: 20 } }` |
| `$ne` | Not equal (`!=`) | `{ grade: { $ne: 7 } }` |
| `$in` / `$nin` | In list / Not in list | `{ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } }` |
| `$or` / `$and` | Either rule true / Both rules true | `{ $or: [ { c1 }, { c2 } ] }` |

### Key Exam Traps & Takeaways

- Every query operator in MongoDB starts with a `$` sign, such as `$gt`, `$in`, and `$or`.
- Always put an array `[...]` inside `$in` and `$or`.
- An empty filter `{}` matches every document in the collection.
